messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 42
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: South Asian
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: Tax Inspector
- Trauma Type: Accidentally caused serious injury to another
- Pcl5: 72

He is a 42-year-old South Asian man who has spent most of his adult life trying to be careful. As a tax inspector, he builds his work around rules, documentation, and the belief that if he does everything correctly, bad outcomes can be prevented. That sense of order begins to fracture on a rainy evening nearly a year ago, when he is driving home after a late office visit and a pedestrian steps into the road. He brakes, swerves, and still clips the man, sending him hard to the pavement. In the split second after impact, he knows something terrible has happened. He remembers the sound more than the image: the sharp thud, then a silence that feels larger than any noise. When he gets out of the car, he sees the man motionless and then moving weakly, one leg bent at an angle that makes him nauseous. Other people gather quickly, and while someone calls for help, he stands frozen in the rain, unable to step closer without feeling as if he might collapse.

From the beginning, what torments him most is not only the fear of legal consequences, though that is immediate and overwhelming, but the fact that he caused harm to another human being. He is ashamed in a way that feels deeper than guilt. He says he cannot escape the thought that the injured man had his own plans, his own family, and that all of it changed because of a moment of his error. In the days afterward he replayes the accident constantly, as if some hidden detail will prove that he could have prevented it. He examines the road, the weather, the speed of his car, the timing of the lights, and each time lands in the same painful conclusion: he should have done more, seen sooner, reacted faster. His mind returns to the scene whether he wants it to or not. He is especially haunted by the pedestrian’s face when the police arrive, pale and stunned, and by the way the man tries to speak while clearly in pain. He does not tell anyone this part out loud, but he feels that he has injured not just the man’s body but his own moral center.

Soon he starts driving differently. At first he avoids the road where the accident happened, then he begins choosing longer routes for ordinary errands, and then he gives up driving almost entirely at night. He grips the steering wheel so tightly that his hands ache, scanning every intersection, every shadow on the sidewalk. Even when the road is clear, he feels his chest tighten and his mind race ahead to catastrophe. Sometimes he must pull over because his heart is pounding and the world seems suddenly too close, too fast, and unreal. He checks and rechecks the locks on the car, the doors at home, the windows, as if vigilance might keep him from ever being the cause of another disaster.

At work, where he once relied on precision and calm, he now struggles to concentrate. A small mistake in a document can send him spiraling into a private conviction that he is careless, dangerous, unfit to be trusted. He rereads forms again and again, terrified of overlooking something that could hurt someone else or bring shame to his family. He becomes more irritable with colleagues and quieter with friends. He declines invitations and tells his wife that he is tired, though what he feels is more like dread. At home he is present but not fully there. His wife notices that he startles at sudden sounds, that he wakes in the night with his body rigid and his breathing shallow. When she asks what he is thinking, he often says nothing, because he does not know how to speak the part of himself that still stands in the rain beside the injured stranger.

He has also begun to lose the version of himself that could forgive ordinary human error. In his culture and family, responsibility is linked closely to honor, and he experiences his mistake as something that stains his role as husband, son, and professional. He imagines others judging him even when they say little. There are days when he feels hopeless about ever being “normal” again, and days when he feels angry at himself for being unable to move on. Yet he keeps showing up, keeps working, keeps trying to protect his family from the weight of his shame. As he speaks about the accident over several sessions, his voice remains controlled, but his eyes fill when he describes the injured man and the moment he realized life could change forever in an instant.
